author: Anton Korinek
title: Scenario Planning for an A(G)I Future
central_scenario_summary: Uncertainty about AI progress is so deep that policymakers should plan across three scenarios—business as usual, AGI in 20 years (labeled 'baseline'), and AGI in 5 years—each with greater than 10% probability. In the AGI scenarios, Korinek-Suh modeling shows output growth accelerating sharply once labor scarcity no longer binds, while competitive wages first rise and then plummet as the economy approaches AGI, because abundant machines substitute for scarce labor. Since the same force drives the output takeoff and the wage collapse, institutions (tax reform, expanded safety nets, small scalable basic incomes) can compensate workers and turn AGI into shared prosperity; policymakers should monitor indicators and adapt as the realized scenario reveals itself.

quotes.text: Scenario II (baseline, AGI in 20 years): Over the next 20 years, AI gradually advances to the point of AGI, resulting in its ability to perform all human work tasks by the end of the period, devaluing labor
I estimate that each of these scenarios has a greater than 10 percent probability of materializing.

expertise_erosion.notes: In the AGI scenarios all human skill premia—including expert work—are competed away as machines master the full task-complexity distribution; erosion is via replacement, not lower entry barriers for humans.

quotes.text: output growth in the two AGI scenarios is much faster, as the scarcity of labor is no longer a constraint on output.

productivity_breadth.notes: Economy-wide transformative gains in the AGI scenarios; business-as-usual scenario retains historical growth.

quotes.text: the takeoff in output and the collapse in wages in the two AGI scenarios are both driven by the same force: the substitution of scarce labor by comparatively more abundant machines.

substitution.notes: Substitution is the explicit central mechanism in the baseline; Scenario I (business as usual) instead features reallocation to more productive jobs.

demand_absorption.notes: No position on demand-side absorption or saturation; wage collapse operates through factor supply, not demand elasticities. He notes society may choose to preserve 'nostalgic' jobs (priests, judges, lawmakers) that 'could sustain demand for human labor in perpetuity'—a caveat, not the central case.

mobility_adjustment.notes: Scenario I assumes workers 'move into new jobs that are, on average, more productive'; in AGI scenarios there is nowhere to reallocate. No position on frictions/retraining speed itself; organizational frictions and regulation are listed only as factors that might slow AGI rollout.

quotes.text: They plummet as the economy is close to reaching AGI.
it should be possible to design institutions that compensate workers for their income losses and ensure that the gains from AGI lead to shared prosperity.

rent_concentration.notes: In the baseline, market income shifts overwhelmingly to capital/machine owners (wage collapse alongside output takeoff); shared prosperity requires deliberate institutional redesign, implying default concentration.

timeline_years.notes: Baseline 20 years to AGI (from 2023); aggressive variant 5 years; each scenario assigned >10% probability.

inequality_prediction.score: In the AGI scenarios, output takes off while competitive wages plummet once labor is no longer scarce, generating potentially extreme inequality between owners of machines/capital and workers across growth, wages, fiscal sustainability, and political stability. But because the same substitution force drives both the output boom and the wage collapse, well-designed institutions—reformed taxation, expanded safety nets, small basic incomes that can be scaled up—can compensate workers and deliver shared prosperity.

This may involve gradual steps, such as reforming systems of taxation and expanding social safety nets, or new programs, such as introducing small basic incomes that can be scaled up when necessary.
